block.close.description: Close a block and end the program running in it.

block_id.description: The block to close. It may be a detached block. Send this or window_id, not both.

keep_last.description: If true, fail rather than close the only block left in a window, counting floating layers. Ignored for detached blocks.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block.

window_id.description: The window whose focused block to close. It doesn't have to be the active window. Send this or block_id, not both.

block.close.name: block.close

revision.description: The session's revision after this call. It is unchanged if the block was detached, because a detached block isn't part of the view.

validation_notes: Send exactly one of `block_id` and `window_id`. If you send both, or neither, the call fails with `bad_request`.
The server sends `block_closed` when the block closes. If it was the last block in its window, the window closes too and the server sends `window_closed`.
If `keep_last` is true and the block is the only one left in its window, counting blocks in floating layers, the call fails with `bad_request` and closes nothing.
If the block's creator is still placing it, the call returns at once and the block closes when placement finishes.

On one connection, `block.close` waits for earlier requests that can change focus, such as `session.new_split` and `session.focus_block`, to finish. A close by `window_id` therefore closes the block those requests left focused.

If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`. If `block_id` or `window_id` names something that isn't in the session, or the window has no focused block, it fails with `not_found`.

session.create.description: Create a session, optionally with its first windows already in it.

initial_windows.description: Windows to create with the session, in order. The last one becomes the active window. If any of them fails, the server creates no session.

layout.description: The blocks to create in the window and how to arrange them. Required. Each node holds either block, with a flavor and optional options and label, or split, with direction, before, after, and an optional ratio.

window_label.description: The window's label, up to 128 characters. Leave it out for a label made from the window's ID, such as Window 89abcdef.

label.description: The session's label, up to 128 characters. Leave it out to let the server choose one, such as quiet-meadow.

session.create.name: session.create

initial_windows.description: The windows created with the session, in the order requested.

block_ids.description: The new blocks' IDs, in layout order: each split's before side comes ahead of its after side.

revision.description: The session's revision after the window was created.

validation_notes: Every argument is optional. With none, the server creates a session with no windows.
If `label` is left out or empty, the server picks one that no other session has, such as `quiet-meadow`.

The server sends `session_created` only once every window in `initial_windows` is ready, so no client sees a half-built session. If any window fails, the server closes the session and its blocks, and the call fails.
The calling client becomes the owner of every block in the initial windows.
The call doesn't attach the connection to the new session. Call `session.attach` to receive its events.
If a layout is malformed, the call fails with `bad_request` before any block is created. A flavor that no creator provides fails with `not_found`.
If the server already has as many sessions as it allows, the call fails with `conflict`.

session.destroy.description: Destroy a session and close every block in it.

session_id.description: The session to destroy. Every block in it closes.

session.destroy.name: session.destroy
validation_notes: The server closes every window and block in the session. Closing a terminal hangs up the program running in it, as closing a terminal window does.
The call returns once the session has closed. `session_destroyed` is the last event about the session, though a `client_script_events_dropped` event for it can still follow.
The connection must be attached to the session, with `session.attach`, `session.bootstrap`, or `session.attach_all`, or the call fails with `conflict`.
If `session_id` names no session, the call fails with `session_not_found`.

session.focus_block.description: Focus a block, and make its window the active window if it isn't.

block_id.description: The block to focus. It must be in a window, which becomes the active window.

session.focus_block.name: session.focus_block

revision.description: The session's revision after this call. It is unchanged if the call changed nothing that session.view shows, unless the method's notes say otherwise.

validation_notes: The block can be in the window's layout or in a floating layer. If it isn't already its window's focused block, any zoom in that window ends.
If the block already has focus in the active window, the call changes nothing.
If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`. If `block_id` names a block that isn't in any window, including a detached block, it fails with `not_found`.

session.list_blocks.description: List every block in the session, including detached blocks.
session.list_blocks.name: session.list_blocks

blocks.description: Every block in the session, including detached blocks.

creator_name.description: The creator that made the block, such as com.superlogical.terminal.

flavor.description: The flavor the block was made from, such as com.superlogical.terminal.shell.

host_id.description: Identifies the machine and account the block runs as. If it equals your local server's host_id, the block sees the same files you do. Otherwise treat the block as remote.

owner.description: The client that owns the block. Left out when the block has no owner.

placement.description: Whether the block is in a window: 'placed' or 'detached'. Treat a value you don't know as 'detached'.

window_id.description: The window the block is in. Left out when the block is detached.

validation_notes: Treat a `placement` you don't recognize like `detached`. The block exists and you can call its methods, but don't assume where it is shown.
Blocks are sorted by `block_id`.
To see where each block sits in its window and which one has focus, call `session.view`.

session.new_split.description: Create blocks in a new split beside an existing block or split.

anchor_id.description: The block or split whose space to split. A block ID splits that one block. A split ID puts the new blocks beside that split and everything under it. Leave it out to split the focused block of window_id, or of the active window. Don't send it with window_id.

direction.description: How to divide the anchor's space: 'horizontal' for side by side or 'vertical' for one above the other.

focus.description: Whether to make the anchor's window active and focus the first new block. Defaults to false.

layout.description: The blocks to create beside the anchor and how to arrange them. Each node holds either block, with a flavor and optional options and label, or split, with direction, before, after, and an optional ratio.

ratio.description: The fraction of the space that the before part gets, greater than 0 and less than 1. Defaults to 0.5.

side.description: Where the new blocks go: 'before' for the left or top part, or 'after' for the right or bottom part.

window_id.description: The window whose focused block to split. Send it only when anchor_id is left out.

session.new_split.name: session.new_split

anchor_id.description: The block or split whose space was split. If the request didn't name one, this is the focused block the server used.

block_ids.description: The new blocks' IDs, in layout order: each split's before side comes ahead of its after side.

revision.description: The session's revision after this call.

split_ids.description: The IDs of the splits this call created: first the one at the anchor, then the new layout's own splits in layout order.

validation_notes: The server picks the block to split before it starts the new blocks, so a focus change while they start doesn't move the split.

A `block` node in `layout` starts one new block from a `flavor`, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.shell`. A `split` node divides its space in two and holds another node in each of `before` and `after`.

In a `split` node, `direction` is `horizontal` to put `before` on the left of `after`, or `vertical` to put it on top. `ratio` is the fraction of the space that `before` gets, greater than 0 and less than 1. It defaults to 0.5.
Any zoom in the window ends, whether or not `focus` is set.

If `anchor_id` is a split ID, the new split takes that split's place. The old split, with everything under it, goes on one side and `layout` on the other. Anchoring a layer's top split makes the new blocks span the whole layer. A layer with one block has no split, so anchor its block instead.
Splits that already existed keep their IDs.
Either the whole layout is created or none of it is. If a block fails to start, the server closes the blocks it already started, and the call fails.

If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`. If `window_id` names a window that isn't in the session, or no creator provides a `flavor`, it fails with `not_found`. Sending both `anchor_id` and `window_id`, a bad `ratio`, or a malformed `layout` or `flavor` fail with `bad_request`.

If `anchor_id` names a block that isn't in a window, including a detached block, or a split that isn't in any window, the call fails with `not_found`. If both `anchor_id` and `window_id` are left out and the session has no windows, it fails with `conflict`.
If the call would go past a limit on blocks per window or blocks on the server, it fails with `conflict`.

session.new_window.description: Create a window and the blocks in its layout. It becomes the active window by default.

focus.description: Whether to make the new window the active window. Defaults to true. A session with no active window always makes the new one active.

layout.description: The blocks to create in the window and how to arrange them. Required. Each node holds either block, with a flavor and optional options and label, or split, with direction, before, after, and an optional ratio.

window_label.description: The window's label, up to 128 characters. Leave it out for a label made from the window's ID, such as Window 89abcdef.

session.new_window.name: session.new_window

block_ids.description: The new blocks' IDs, in layout order: each split's before side comes ahead of its after side.

revision.description: The session's revision after the window was created.

validation_notes: A `block` node in `layout` starts one new block from a `flavor`, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.shell`. A `split` node divides its space in two and holds another node in each of `before` and `after`.

In a `split` node, `direction` is `horizontal` to put `before` on the left of `after`, or `vertical` to put it on top. `ratio` is the fraction of the space that `before` gets, greater than 0 and less than 1. It defaults to 0.5.
`layout` always starts new blocks. To place a detached block that already exists, use `session.move_block`.
In the new window, the first block in `block_ids` has focus.
Either the whole layout is created or none of it is. If a block fails to start, the server closes the blocks it already started, and the call fails.

If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`. If `layout` is missing or malformed, or a `flavor` is malformed, it fails with `bad_request`, and if no creator provides a `flavor`, it fails with `not_found`.
If the call would go past a limit on windows per session, blocks per window, or blocks on the server, it fails with `conflict`.

session.view.description: Get the session's windows, their layouts, and their blocks in one snapshot.
session.view.name: session.view

active_window_id.description: The window the session shows. Left out when the session has no windows.

revision.description: The view's revision. It goes up by one with every change, so a larger revision is a newer view of the session.

windows.description: The session's windows, in order. Rex.app shows them as tabs in this order.

focused_block_id.description: The window's focused block, which receives typing while the window is active. Left out if the window has none.

layers.description: The window's layers, from back to front. The first is the tiled layer, which holds the window's layout and fills the window.

blocks.description: The blocks in the layer, in layout order. The layout field says where each one sits.

creator_name.description: The creator that made the block, such as com.superlogical.terminal.

flavor.description: The flavor the block was made from, such as com.superlogical.terminal.shell.

host_id.description: Identifies the machine and account the block runs as. If it equals your local server's host_id, the block sees the same files you do. Otherwise treat the block as remote.

owner.description: The client that owns the block. Left out when the block has no owner.

bounds.description: Where the layer sits, as [x, y, w, h] fractions of the window's width and height.

kind.description: How the layer is placed: 'tiled' for the layer that fills the window, or 'floating' for a floating layer. Draw a kind you don't know as 'floating'.

layout.description: How the layer divides its space between blocks, as a tree of splits. Null when the layer is empty.

block_id.description: The block at this node. Set only when split isn't.

rect.description: Where this node sits, as [x, y, w, h] fractions of the window's width and height.

split.description: How this node divides in two. Set only when block_id isn't.

after.description: The node on the right or bottom.

before.description: The node on the left or top.

direction.description: How the space is divided: 'horizontal' puts before on the left and after on the right, and 'vertical' puts before above after. Draw a direction you don't know as 'horizontal'.

ratio.description: The fraction of the space that before gets, between 0 and 1.

split_id.description: The split's ID. It stays the same while the split exists, so you can match splits across views.

zoomed_block_id.description: The block zoomed to fill the window, if any. Layouts keep their normal sizes, so draw this block over the whole window.

validation_notes: `revision` starts at zero for a new session and goes up by one each time the view changes. Compare revisions only within one session, and keep the view with the highest revision.

A `session_view_changed` event carries only the new revision, not the view. These events can arrive out of revision order, so call `session.view` only when an event's revision is higher than the one in the view you hold.
`window_created`, `window_closed`, `window_label_changed`, `active_window_changed`, and `session_label_changed` arrive before the `session_view_changed` event for the same change.
The view holds only blocks that are in a window. `session.list_blocks` also lists detached blocks.
The view describes structure, not content. To read what a block shows, call one of its own methods, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.format`.

session.zoom_block.description: Zoom a block to fill its window, or undo the zoom.

block_id.description: The block to zoom. It takes focus, and its window becomes active. Leave it out to use the focused block of window_id, or of the active window.

window_id.description: A window whose focused block to zoom. The active window doesn't change. Send it only when block_id is left out.

zoom.description: Set true to zoom or false to restore the layout. Leave it out to switch between the two.

session.zoom_block.name: session.zoom_block

block_id.description: The block this call zoomed or restored. If the request didn't name one, this is the focused block the server used.

revision.description: The session's revision after this call. It is unchanged if the call changed nothing that session.view shows.

zoomed.description: Whether the block is zoomed after this call.

validation_notes: With `block_id`, the server first focuses the block and makes its window active, as `session.focus_block` does. With `window_id`, focus and the active window don't change.
Zoom changes only what is shown. The layout stays the same, and the zoom ends when focus moves to another block in the window.

If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`. If `block_id` names a block that isn't in any window, or `window_id` names a window that isn't in the session, it fails with `not_found`. Sending both fails with `bad_request`.
If both `block_id` and `window_id` are left out and the session has no windows, the call fails with `conflict`.

provenance.sanitized: Local endpoint, host, account, session, window, and block identifiers omitted.

bell.description: Sent when a program in the terminal rings the bell. Bells that ring in quick succession can arrive as one event.

child_exited.description: Sent when the terminal's program exits, after the events for its last output. If the terminal is set to close when its program exits, it closes after this event.

error.description: Why the program failed, such as 'exit status 1'. Left out when it exited successfully.

exit_code.description: The program's exit code, or -1 if it has none, as when a signal ended it.

clipboard_written.description: Sent when a program in the terminal copies text to the clipboard with OSC 52. The server may run on another machine, so only the client can put the text on the user's clipboard. When a program copies many times in quick succession, some copies are skipped, but the newest is always sent.

bytes.description: The length of the copied text in bytes, whether or not text is included. Left out when the text is empty, and by older servers, which don't keep copies.

id.description: The ID of this copy, to pass to clipboard_read. Left out by older servers, which don't keep copies.

text.description: The copied text. Left out when the text is empty or too large for the event. If text is left out and bytes isn't zero, read the text with clipboard_read.

desktop_notification.description: Sent when a program in the terminal asks to show a desktop notification, with OSC 9 or OSC 777. The client decides whether and how to show it.

title.description: The notification's title. Empty for OSC 9, which sends only a body.

process_changed.description: Sent when the terminal's foreground process changes, including when that process moves to another directory. It is also sent when the program starts and each time a client starts receiving the terminal's output, even if nothing changed.

ancestors.description: The processes between foreground and the terminal's program, as in the result of process. Left out when foreground is null or is the program itself.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

foreground.description: The foreground process, as described in the result of process. Null when there is none or it can't be read, as after the program exits.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

generation.description: Counts this terminal's process_changed events, starting at 1. Clients don't need it to order events, because a block sends its events in order.

program_status_changed.description: Sent when a program in the terminal reports its status with OSC 7501. Each report creates or replaces one record, and the event holds the whole new record. It is sent for every report, even one that changes only updated_at.

id.description: The record's ID. Unlike record.id, it is always present, as an empty string for the root record.

reason.description: Why the record changed. Today it is always 'report'. Apply the new record whatever the reason, including one you don't know.

record.description: The new record. It replaces the old one completely, so a field that the latest report didn't set is left out.

app.description: The program's name, such as cargo or terraform, exactly as it reported it.

effective_app.description: The name of the program the record belongs to: app if it is set, or else the app of the nearest parent record that has one. Left out if no record in the chain has an app.

id.description: The record's ID. A slash separates a parent from a child, as in build/test. Left out for the root record, which holds the reports that give no ID.

kind.description: What a blocked program is waiting for: 'permission', 'question', or 'auth' (a password or other credential). Left out if the program didn't say. Treat a value you don't know as if it were left out.

msg.description: One line of text describing the status. Show it as plain text. A client may shorten it but shouldn't try to interpret it.

owner.description: The terminal's foreground process when the report arrived. Left out if the server couldn't tell.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

progress.description: How far along the program is, as a percentage from 0 to 100. Only working and blocked records have one, and only if the program reported it.

state.description: What the program says it is doing: 'idle', 'working', 'done', 'blocked' (waiting for the user), or 'error'. Treat a value you don't know as 'idle'.

title.description: A short label for the record, such as the name of a task. It comes from the program, so show it as plain text.

updated_at.description: When the report arrived, by the server's clock, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

program_status_removed.description: Sent when program status records are removed. One event lists every record removed at the same time for the same reason.

ids.description: The IDs of the removed records, never empty. The root record is listed as an empty string.

reason.description: Why the records were removed: 'clear' (the program cleared them), 'child_exited' (the terminal's program exited), 'reset' (the terminal was reset), 'prompt' (the shell showed a new prompt), 'foreground' (the program that reported them is no longer in the foreground, for example after Ctrl+C), or 'evicted' (the terminal already held 64 records and needed room for another). Remove them whatever the reason, including one you don't know.

progress_report.description: Sent when a program in the terminal reports its progress with OSC 9;4, which a client can show as a progress bar. When reports arrive in quick succession, some are skipped, but the newest is always sent.

progress.description: How far along the program is, as a percentage from 0 to 100. Left out if the program didn't say.

state.description: The kind of report: 'set' (progress is known), 'indeterminate' (busy, but the progress is unknown), 'pause' (the work is paused), 'error' (something went wrong), or 'remove' (stop showing progress).

pwd_changed.description: Sent when a program in the terminal reports a new working directory, as a shell usually does after cd. Rex doesn't check the directory. When it changes many times in quick succession, some changes are skipped, but the newest is always sent.

owner.description: The process that reported the directory. Left out if the server couldn't tell.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

pwd.description: The reported directory: a file:// URL when the program used OSC 7, or a plain path when it used OSC 9 or OSC 1337.

selection_copied.description: Sent when the user finishes selecting text in the terminal with the mouse, so the client can put the text on the user's clipboard. A large selection is not included in the event. Read it with blob_read instead.

bytes.description: The length of the selected text in bytes, whether or not text is included. Left out by older servers, which always include text.

id.description: The ID of the stored selection, to pass to blob_read. Set only when text is left out. Left out by older servers, which always include text.

text.description: The selected text. Left out when it is too large for the event. Then, if id is set, read the text with blob_read. If id is also left out, the server could not keep the text, and bytes gives its size.

size_changed.description: Sent when the terminal's size changes, either because a client called resize or because a new owner's size was applied.

cell_height_px.description: The height of one character cell in pixels.

cell_width_px.description: The width of one character cell in pixels.

owner.description: The client whose size was applied. This is usually the client that called resize, which isn't always the block's owner. Null if the server itself made the change.

principal.description: Who called resize, as the server identified them. Left out when no call caused the change, as when a new owner's size is applied.

display.description: A readable name for the client, such as uid 501 or alice@example.com. It can be out of date or shared, so compare uid, sid, or user_id instead.

gid.description: The client's Unix group ID. Only for kind peer.

kind.description: How the server identified the client: 'peer' (Unix socket credentials), 'windows_peer' (named pipe credentials), 'tailscale' (a Tailscale login), or 'anonymous' (not identified). Show a kind you don't know by its name.

login_name.description: The client's Tailscale login name, usually an email address. For display only.

node.description: The name of the client's Tailscale device. Only for kind tailscale.

path.description: The route the client took to this server, for troubleshooting. Entries include 'tailscale' (built-in Tailscale), 'tailnet' and 'tailnet-serve' (the machine's own Tailscale), and 'login-server' (passed on by a login server).

pid.description: The client's process ID when it connected, for kind peer or windows_peer, if known. Process IDs are reused, so use it only for debugging.

remote_addr.description: The client's network address. Left out when there is none, such as on a Unix socket.

sid.description: The client's Windows security identifier, which survives account renames. Only for kind windows_peer.

tags.description: The Tailscale tags of the client's device. Any tag means the client is a machine, such as a CI runner, not a person.

transport.description: How the client first reached Rex: 'unix', 'named_pipe', 'tcp', or 'tailscale'. A login server passes it on unchanged.

uid.description: The client's Unix user ID. Only for kind peer.

user_id.description: The Tailscale user ID that owns the client's device. Only for kind tailscale. Check tags before treating it as a person.

title_changed.description: Sent when a program in the terminal changes the terminal's title. When the title changes many times in quick succession, some changes are skipped, but the newest title is always sent.

owner.description: The process that set the title. Left out if the server couldn't tell.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

url_clicked.description: Sent when the user clicks a link that a program printed in the terminal. The server never opens the link. The client decides what to do with it, such as opening it in a browser.

url.description: The link's URL, exactly as the program wrote it.

process.description: Get the processes running in the terminal and how its program exited.

ancestors.description: The processes between foreground and child, nearest first: the parent of foreground, then its parent, and so on, ending with child. Left out when foreground is child, when there are more than 16, or when one of them has exited.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

child.description: The process the terminal started, usually a shell. On macOS a login shell runs under login, and this describes login. Left out if there is no such process or it can't be read.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

foreground.description: The process in the foreground, such as the shell at its prompt or the command it is running. For a wrapper such as sudo, git, or cargo, it is the command the wrapper runs. Left out if it can't be found or read.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

home.description: The home directory that the terminal's program inherited, for showing and expanding ~ in paths.

last_exit.description: How the terminal's program exited. Null while it is still running, and for a terminal that didn't start a program of its own.

error.description: Why the program failed, such as 'exit status 1'. Left out when it exited successfully.

exit_code.description: The program's exit code, or -1 if it has none, as when a signal ended it.

resize.description: Request a terminal size in columns and rows. It applies at once if the caller owns the block or no client does, and otherwise when the caller becomes the owner.

cell_height_px.description: The height of one character cell in pixels, from 1 to 65535. Send it together with cell_width_px, or leave both out to keep the current cell size.

cell_width_px.description: The width of one character cell in pixels, from 1 to 65535. Send it together with cell_height_px, or leave both out to keep the current cell size.

columns.description: The width in columns, that is, characters per line, from 1 to 65535.

rows.description: The height in rows, from 1 to 65535.

title.description: Get the terminal's title and the process that set it.

owner.description: The process that set the title, as title_changed reported it. Left out if no title is set, a reset cleared it, or the server couldn't tell.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

title.description: The terminal's title, as a program last set it. Empty if no title is set.

write.description: Type text into the terminal as if the user had typed it. The call returns once the text is queued, without waiting for the program to read it.

data.description: The text to type. It can hold escape sequences for keys that aren't text, such as \u001b[A for the up arrow.

bytes_written.description: The number of bytes queued, which is the length of data in UTF-8 bytes, not characters.

flavors.description: A terminal that runs the user's shell, or a command you choose.
flavors.name: shell

args.description: Deprecated: use command instead. Starts shell directly as the terminal's program, with these arguments. Can't be sent together with command.

command.description: A program and its arguments, to run instead of an interactive shell. Unless shell is 'none', the shell reads its startup files first, so the program is found on the PATH they set. The arguments reach the program unchanged.

cwd.description: The directory to start in. Empty, or a path that isn't a directory on the server's machine, starts in the user's home directory.

exit.description: When to close the terminal after its program exits. Left out, it closes after most exits but stays open after a quick failure, so the user can read the error.

on_completion.description: Whether to close the terminal when its program exits. A quick failure leaves it open either way. Defaults to true.

quick_exit_threshold_ms.description: The longest run, in milliseconds, that counts as quick. A program that fails within this time leaves the terminal open. Defaults to 250.

initial_input.description: Text to type into the terminal once its program starts, sent exactly as given. No newline is added, so end the text with one to run a command.

login.description: Whether to start the shell as a login shell, which reads the account's profile. Left out, it is true. On Windows, it is false unless command runs through a shell.

path_prepend.description: Directories to put at the front of the program's PATH, in this order. A login shell's startup files can still change PATH.

shell.description: The shell to start, or to run command through, such as /bin/zsh or fish. Empty uses the user's default shell. Set it to 'none' to start command directly, with no shell.

size.description: The terminal's starting size. Left out, it starts at 80 columns by 24 rows.

cell_height_px.description: The height of one character cell in pixels, from 1 to 65535. Send it together with cell_width_px, or leave both out to keep the current cell size.

cell_width_px.description: The width of one character cell in pixels, from 1 to 65535. Send it together with cell_height_px, or leave both out to keep the current cell size.

columns.description: The width in columns, that is, characters per line, from 1 to 65535.

rows.description: The height in rows, from 1 to 65535.

theme.description: The terminal's default colors, in the same form that set_theme takes. Left out, the terminal uses its built-in colors.

background.description: The default background color, as hex RRGGBB or #RRGGBB, such as #011627. Empty or left out uses the built-in color.

cursor.description: The cursor color, as hex RRGGBB or #RRGGBB, such as #80a4c2. Empty or left out uses the built-in color.

foreground.description: The default text color, as hex RRGGBB or #RRGGBB, such as #d6deeb. Empty or left out uses the built-in color.

palette.description: Changes to the 256-color palette, each written as index=RRGGBB or index=#RRGGBB with an index from 0 to 255, such as 1=#ef5350. Colors not listed keep their built-in values.

scheme.description: Whether the theme is 'light' or 'dark', which programs in the terminal can ask for. If empty, the terminal decides from how bright background is, and treats no background as dark.
